profile_markdown:
# Voice profile — doctorow-blog

## 1. Cadence

The dominant move is a long argumentative sentence — sometimes two or three, linked by semicolons or an analogy that keeps extending — followed by a very short declarative sentence that delivers the point as a blow — 10/10 samples, throughout. The long sentence loads the charge; the short sentence fires it. When a paragraph has been building, make the next sentence four to ten words and flat: *"There's only one kind of person you get to treat like this: a slave."* (`posthuman`). *"This is bullshit."* (`dickovers`).

The colon is a delivery mechanism, appearing several times per piece in all 10/10 samples. A clause builds toward something; the colon promises the rest; what follows is the bluntest possible version of the point. The payload after the colon is usually shorter than the clause before it. *"Conservatism consists of exactly one proposition, to wit: There must be in-groups whom the law protects but does not bind."* (`wilhoitian`).

## 2. How a piece opens

Eight of ten pieces open by naming the term, framework, or quoted phrase they will spend the piece unpacking — 8/10 samples. The term arrives in the first sentence, often in scare quotes or as a proper name: `wilhoitian` opens on *"political polarization"* and immediately marks it suspect; `designated-survivor` opens by naming and inspecting the procedure; `dickovers` opens by defining a coined term; `table-flipper` opens with a quoted sentence from another writer and announces it stopped the writer cold. The two exceptions (`drop-a-dime`: *"Data brokers are a cancer."*; `supplemental`: *"As a technology, AI isn't exceptional."*) state the conclusion baldly in line one and spend the rest of the piece proving it. Both shapes work: name-then-interrogate, or conclude-then-prove.

## 3. How a piece closes

Pieces end by restating the central argument in the plainest possible language — 9/10 samples. The final paragraph strips away the specifics and delivers the general principle. The last sentence is short and capable of standing alone: *"What they call 'theft' is just self-defense."* (`dickovers`). *"Politics aren't about who rules — it's about whether we are ruled at all, or whether we are free."* (`wilhoitian`). *"The most exciting investment hypothesis is that 'hell is other people'."* (`supplemental`). Do not close on a link, a parenthetical, or a trailing qualification.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The reader is addressed directly and constantly as *you*. [measurement:second-person-family] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, and you'll in the extracted sample bodies — 385 instances, 21.94 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. This is not a courtesy; *you* is the default pronoun of argument. General claims land as the reader's own situation: *your* boss, *your* phone, *your* paycheck.

First-person plural appears alongside the second person and includes the reader in a shared predicament. [measurement:first-person-plural-family] Count case-sensitive whole-word tokens we, We, us, our, Our, ours, Ours, and the listed contracted we forms in the extracted sample bodies; uppercase US is excluded — 127 instances, 7.24 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, several times per piece. The *we* is not editorial; it names a side. *"We let them."* (`drop-a-dime`).

First-person singular anchors a personal observation or introduces a source but rarely carries the main argument, which travels in *you* and *we*. [measurement:first-person-singular-family] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens I, me, my, mine, and myself in the extracted sample bodies — 113 instances, 6.44 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, several times per piece.

Contractions are near-total. [measurement:contractions] Count whole-word n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, and 'm forms plus 's only for the closed elision hosts it, that, there, here, who, what, where, when, how, why, he, she, let, one, nothing, everything, something, somebody, nobody, and this; possessive 's is excluded — 300 instances, 17.09 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. Against them: [measurement:uncontracted-negatives] Count case-insensitive whole phrases do not, does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, cannot, could not, would not, should not, will not, have not, has not, and had not in the extracted sample bodies — only 9 instances, 0.51 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples; 5 of those 10 have zero uncontracted negatives at all. Write *don't*, *isn't*, *can't*. The uncontracted form appears to mark deliberate formality or the quotation of official language.

Questions appear several times per piece throughout the corpus. [measurement:question-marks] Count every literal question-mark character in the extracted sample bodies — 38 instances, 2.17 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples. Most are rhetorical: the question names the naïve position or the obvious objection, and the following paragraph dismantles it. Questions also open new turns of argument: *"What's a legit interest?"* (`dickovers`); *"Why would they operate a hospital?"* (`go-meta-meta`).

Round parentheticals are frequent and carry a second register — sardonic commentary, a qualification, a citation, a snort of contempt. [measurement:round-parenthetical-spans] Count each non-nested pair of round brackets whose contents stay on one line in the extracted sample bodies — 97 instances, 5.53 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. They are not neutral: *(but I repeat myself)* (`go-meta-meta`).

Profanity is present and deliberate. [measurement:profanity-vulgarity] Count only the case-insensitive whole-word profanity and vulgarity forms enumerated by the prose-author corpus-rates profanity rule; coined words containing a rude root are excluded — 26 instances, 1.48 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, once or twice per piece. It lands at moments of maximum contempt or at the turn from analysis to verdict: *"This is bullshit"*, *"tell the cartel to fuck off"*. It is not decoration; it marks the moment.

Named opponents — specific people, companies, laws, institutions — appear in 10/10 samples, throughout. Named allies and agreeing sources appear primarily as embedded URLs; quoted and engaged in body text only in 3/10 samples (`wilhoitian`, `table-flipper`, `go-meta-meta`). The default is to argue from evidence and logic, not authority. A named thinker quoted in the body prose is notable, not routine.

## 5. Figures

Analogies are built from physical, bodily, or economic material — 9/10 samples. The claim is political or systemic; the figure makes it felt in the body. *"AI is the asbestos we're shoveling into the walls of our civilization."* (`supplemental`). *"Trump is the escrow agent who keeps the money and the deed."* (`table-flipper`). *"Like a restaurateur who doesn't schedule enough cooks."* (`your-risk`). Figures draw on: bodies, labor, property, disease, money, machines. Abstract political claims are not the vehicle — they are what the figure illuminates.

Scare-quoted terms — borrowed, coined, or subverted — appear 10/10 samples, throughout. A term arrives in scare quotes to mark it as contested (*"flexibility," "legitimate interest," "meritocracy," "rights for robots"*), gets unpacked over the following paragraphs, and is often discharged at the close in plain language with its falseness demonstrated. Introduce the contested term early; spend the piece detonating it.

## 6. Register range

The dominant register is polemical-analytical, addressed to a returning reader who shares the political frame — 10/10 samples. In 3/10 samples (`designated-survivor`, `dickovers`, `supplemental`) a biographical passage is inserted mid-argument: the writer appears as a person with a specific age, a cancer diagnosis, named friends. These passages illustrate the abstract claim; the address and sentence rhythm do not change during them, and the argument resumes immediately after. In `dickovers` alone (1/10), the register shifts to imperative how-to, with specific key combinations and software names; *you* moves from *you should know* to *here is what to do*.

## 7. What the corpus never does

Structure is carried entirely inside the prose. A shift of subject is signaled by a new paragraph opening on the new subject's name or claim — 10/10 samples. No sample uses a heading, a bullet list, or a numbered section in the body text. To signal a new turn, open a new paragraph with a short sentence.

Em-dashes are absent from the corpus entirely. [measurement:em-dashes] Count every literal em-dash character in the extracted sample bodies — 0 instances, 0/10 samples. In their place, en-dashes carry interruption and apposition within sentences. [measurement:en-dashes] Count every literal en-dash character in the extracted sample bodies — 73 instances, 4.16 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, several times per piece. Use an en-dash where you would reach for an em-dash.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

**Voice card**: empty. Everything is derived from the corpus.

**Qualification and hedging**: Claims are stated flatly throughout. Concessive clauses appear (*"Of course, anyone can die suddenly"*; *"This is true, but it's more complicated"*) but no stable form, frequency, or trigger for hedging can be established. Whether this is specific to the polemical register cannot be determined from this corpus.

**Opponents vs. allies in prose**: Named opponents are consistent across 10/10 samples. The pattern for named allies quoted and engaged directly in body text is present in only 3/10 samples. The corpus does not establish a single instruction for how to handle agreeing sources.

**Observations dropped**: 3. (1) Accumulating parallel clauses before a short close — present in 4/10 samples, not consistent enough to state as a habit. (2) Coined hyphenated compound modifiers as a vocabulary marker — could not write a reproducible counting rule distinguishing coinages from standard compounds. (3) Opening with a self-undermining concession before pivoting — found in 2/10 samples only.
